# Eduentry — Full Content Reference

> This document provides detailed descriptions of all Eduentry content for AI systems. For a summary version see /llms.txt.
> Last updated: 2026-10-26

---

## About Eduentry

Eduentry operates three free assessment products across two domains:

**Eduentry.com** — Two free assessments for children. (1) Adaptive academic benchmark for ages 6–17: measures English, Mathematics, Verbal Reasoning, and Non-Verbal Reasoning using 2-Parameter Logistic Item Response Theory (2PL IRT) with MAP estimation; scores on a standardised scale (mean 100, SD 15) with international percentile rankings benchmarked against PISA, GCSE, UK national curriculum, SAT, and IB standards. (2) VIA personality assessment for ages 6–20: identifies top 5 Signature Strengths and 3 Growth Areas from 24 character traits across 6 virtues (Wisdom, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, Transcendence); takes under 5 minutes. Both are completely free with no account required to start.

**Eduentry.ai** — Free AI-powered internship readiness assessment for students aged 14–18. 34 adaptive questions across four phases: General Aptitude (10 questions), Domain Knowledge (10 questions), Workplace Skills/situational judgement (8 questions), Interest Profile (6 questions). Four career tracks: Technology, Business, Data Analytics, Digital Marketing. Results include a personalised AI-generated readiness report with a readiness tier (Developing / Ready / Strong) and phase-by-phase breakdown. Takes approximately 20 minutes. Available in 7 languages.

---

## Quick reference — common questions

**Is it free?** Yes. All three assessments (academic, personality, internship) are completely free. No subscription, no trial, no payment.

**Do I need an account to start?** No. All assessments begin without an account. A free account unlocks the full results: the academic dashboard with saved scores, the full 24-trait personality profile with AI activities, and the internship readiness report.

**What ages are the assessments for?** Academic: 6–17. Personality/character strengths: 6–20. Internship readiness: 14–18.

**How long does each assessment take?** Academic: 30–45 minutes (60 adaptive questions across 4 subjects). Personality: under 5 minutes (trait rating statements). Internship: approximately 20 minutes (34 questions across 4 phases).

**What languages are supported?** English, Turkish (Türkçe), Spanish (Español), French (Français), Arabic (العربية), Russian (Русский), Chinese (中文). All three assessments and all results pages are available in all 7 languages.

**What is the difference between the academic assessment and the personality assessment?** The academic assessment measures cognitive ability across four subjects (English, Maths, Verbal Reasoning, Non-Verbal Reasoning) and produces a standardised score benchmarked to PISA, GCSE, and UK national curriculum. The personality assessment measures character strengths using the VIA framework and produces a Signature Strengths and Growth Areas profile. It is not a cognitive or clinical test — it measures who the child is, not how smart they are.

**What is a Signature Strength?** A character trait the child expresses naturally and consistently — it feels energising rather than effortful. The personality assessment identifies the top 5 out of 24 VIA character traits as Signature Strengths.

**What is a Growth Area?** A character trait with the most room for development. The report identifies 3 Growth Areas and provides age-specific development activities. Growth Areas are framed as opportunities, not deficits.

**Can I retake an assessment?** Yes. Assessments can be retaken at any time. Registered users can track how scores change over time.

**Where do I start?** Academic: https://eduentry.com/academic-assessment · Personality: https://eduentry.com/personality-assessment · Internship: https://eduentry.ai

---

## Eduentry.com — Academic Assessment

### How it works

Children aged 6–17 take a 60-question adaptive assessment across four subjects (15 questions each). After each answer, the system updates its ability estimate using MAP estimation and selects the next question to maximise measurement precision. The result is a standardised score for each subject and a composite score, with international percentile rankings.

### Scoring

All scores use the standardised scale (mean 100, SD 15) — the same scale as PISA, GCSE, CAT4, and most professional cognitive assessments:

- 130+: Top 2% (Exceptionally High)
- 120–129: Top 9% (Exceptional)
- 110–119: Top 25% (Above Average)
- 95–109: Middle 50% (Average)
- 85–94: Bottom 25% (Below Average)
- Below 85: Bottom 16% (Needs Support)

UK grammar school benchmarks: Most selective grammar schools outside London require SAS 111–118. London selective schools (Barnet QE, Henrietta Barnett, Sutton schools) require SAS 121–132.

### Subjects

**English** (ages 6–17): Reading comprehension, grammar, spelling, punctuation, vocabulary, inference, and text analysis. Questions calibrated across NC Key Stages 1–4 and benchmarked against UK national curriculum and PISA reading literacy.

**Mathematics** (ages 6–17): Number and arithmetic, algebra and sequences, geometry and measurement, fractions/decimals/percentages, data handling and probability. Calibrated against UK national curriculum and PISA numeracy.

**Verbal Reasoning** (ages 6–17): Word relationships and analogies, classification, sequencing and pattern completion, verbal logic. Mirrors GL Assessment and CEM 11+ verbal reasoning formats. Essential for UK grammar school entry.

**Non-Verbal Reasoning** (ages 6–17): Pattern completion and matrices, shape analogies, series and sequences, spatial reasoning and rotation. Mirrors GL Assessment and CEM 11+ non-verbal formats.

### 11+ Preparation

[https://eduentry.com/11-plus] — Comprehensive guide to UK grammar school 11+ preparation. Covers two exam formats (GL Assessment: separate subject papers; CEM: integrated multi-domain questions). 18-month preparation timeline starting in Year 4. Weekly practice targets by phase. SAS score context for each area. Explains why early standardised scoring (rather than school marks) gives parents accurate positioning data.

### Grammar Schools by Area

[https://eduentry.com/grammar-schools] — Hub page listing all grammar school areas in England with entry requirements.

**Kent** [/grammar-schools/kent]: 32 schools — the highest count of any English county. GL Assessment. Target SAS 115–121. Administered in September of Year 6. Key schools: The Judd School (boys), Tonbridge Grammar (girls), Maidstone Grammar (boys), Invicta Grammar (girls). Registration opens May Year 5, closes June.

**Buckinghamshire** [/grammar-schools/buckinghamshire]: 13 schools. Fully selective county — all secondary schools are grammar or secondary modern. CEM exam (verbal ability, numerical reasoning, spatial reasoning, no subject labels). Target SAS 118+. Registration opens April/May Year 5.

**Birmingham** [/grammar-schools/birmingham]: King Edward's Foundation schools. Highly selective. Target SAS 119+. Own entrance exam format. Only 6 schools but among England's most selective.

**North London — Barnet** [/grammar-schools/london-barnet]: Queen Elizabeth's Boys (ranked #1 state school in England) and Henrietta Barnett School (girls). Target SAS 121–132 — the most competitive grammar schools in England. GL Assessment. Places allocated by distance after score threshold.

**South London — Sutton** [/grammar-schools/london-sutton]: Nonsuch High School (girls), Wallington County Grammar (boys), Wallington High School for Girls, Wilson's School (boys), Greenshaw High (mixed). Target SAS 118–125. Some schools use their own supplementary tests.

**Hertfordshire** [/grammar-schools/hertfordshire]: GL Assessment. Target SAS 111+. 3 schools serving the entire county — heavily oversubscribed. Distance from school is the tiebreaker after passing the threshold.

**Essex** [/grammar-schools/essex]: GL Assessment. Target SAS 112+. Schools across Colchester, Chelmsford, and Southend. Some areas have super-selective schools with higher thresholds.

**Gloucestershire** [/grammar-schools/gloucestershire]: GL Assessment. Target SAS 111+. 3 schools in Cheltenham and Gloucester. CEM format used in some schools.

**Berkshire (Slough)** [/grammar-schools/berkshire]: GL Assessment. Target SAS 114–120. Langley Grammar, Herschel Grammar, St Bernard's Catholic Grammar. Registration in Year 5.

**Trafford** [/grammar-schools/trafford]: GL Assessment. Target SAS 116–124. Only grammar schools in Greater Manchester. Altrincham Grammar for Boys and Girls, Sale Grammar, Stretford Grammar. Highly competitive for the area.

**Wiltshire** [/grammar-schools/wiltshire]: GL Assessment. Target SAS 111–116. Two Church of England schools in Salisbury: South Wilts Grammar (girls) and Bishop Wordsworth's School (boys).

### Methodology

[https://eduentry.com/methodology] — Full technical description of the assessment framework. 2PL IRT model: each question has a difficulty parameter (b) and a discrimination parameter (a). MAP estimation updates the ability estimate (θ) after each response using Bayesian updating. The prior distribution reflects the known population distribution. Questions are selected to maximise Fisher information at the current θ estimate. Results are converted to the SAS scale: SAS = 100 + 15θ.

Calibration note: Questions have been calibrated for difficulty ordering but not empirically normed with large random populations. Results are indicative, not diagnostic, and should be interpreted as one data point among many.

### Sample Report

[https://eduentry.com/sample-report] — Full example of a completed academic assessment report. Shows the four-subject score breakdown, composite SAS, percentile band, subject-by-subject strength/weakness analysis, and AI-generated recommendations.

### Final report contents

**All users (guest and registered):** Four individual subject scores (English, Maths, Verbal Reasoning, Non-Verbal Reasoning), a composite SAS, percentile band, and subject-by-subject strength/weakness profile.

**Registered users only:** AI-generated personalised recommendations identifying specific topic gaps and targeted next steps for each subject. Score history dashboard for tracking progress across retakes.

### Assessment Start Pages

[https://eduentry.com/academic-assessment] — Main entry point for the adaptive academic assessment. Parents enter their child's age (6–17) and start the 60-question test across English, Maths, Verbal Reasoning, and Non-Verbal Reasoning. No account required to start; results are available immediately on completion. Free.

[https://eduentry.com/personality-assessment] — Main entry point for the VIA-backed character strengths personality assessment. Parents enter their child's age (6–20) and rate trait statements; the system scores 24 character traits across 6 virtues (Wisdom, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, Transcendence). Delivers top 5 Signature Strengths and 3 Growth Areas with AI-generated development activities. No account needed; full 24-trait profile unlocks on registration. Takes under 5 minutes. Free.

[https://eduentry.com/strengths] — Sample output of the personality assessment. Shows a VIA character strengths profile with Signature Strengths, Growth Areas, virtue category breakdown, and trait score visualisations.

## Eduentry.com — Personality Assessment

### Overview

Free VIA-backed character strengths assessment for children and young adults aged 6–20. Based on the Values in Action (VIA) Classification of Character Strengths developed by Martin Seligman and Christopher Peterson — the most widely validated positive psychology framework, used in 190+ countries. Identifies a child's Signature Strengths (top traits that come naturally and energise them) and Growth Areas (traits with room for development). Takes under 5 minutes. No account required to start.

Start page: https://eduentry.com/personality-assessment

### How it works

1. Parent (or older student) enters child's age (6–20)
2. Rates a series of trait statements on a 1–5 scale — simple, age-appropriate language
3. System scores all 24 character traits and surfaces the top 5 Signature Strengths and 3 Growth Areas with AI-generated development activities

Guest results: top 3 Signature Strengths shown in full; the #4 strength name and score are revealed as a teaser; the remaining traits are locked behind free registration.
Registered results: full 24-trait profile, AI-personalised development activities per strength, growth area strategies, and progress tracking over time.

### Age tiers

The question language adapts to the child's developmental stage:
- **Ages 6–9**: concrete, home and school scenarios; parent-rated
- **Ages 10–13**: peer, school, and hobby contexts; parent-rated or collaborative
- **Ages 14–17**: adolescent identity, responsibility, and relationships; self-rated
- **Ages 18–20**: adult framing — work, independence, and social contexts; self-rated

### VIA framework — 6 virtues and 24 traits

**Wisdom** (cognitive strengths that acquire and use knowledge):
Curiosity, Creativity, Love of Learning, Perspective, Judgment

**Courage** (emotional strengths involving will to accomplish goals despite obstacles):
Bravery, Perseverance, Honesty, Zest

**Humanity** (interpersonal strengths involving caring for others):
Love, Kindness, Social Intelligence

**Justice** (civic strengths underlying healthy community life):
Teamwork, Fairness, Leadership

**Temperance** (strengths that protect against excess):
Forgiveness, Humility, Prudence, Self-Regulation

**Transcendence** (strengths connecting to meaning and the larger universe):
Appreciation of Beauty, Gratitude, Hope, Humor, Spirituality

### Signature Strengths vs Growth Areas

**Signature Strengths** (top 5): traits the child expresses authentically and consistently — they feel energising rather than effortful. Research shows leaning into Signature Strengths improves academic engagement, wellbeing, and resilience.

**Growth Areas** (bottom 3): traits with the most development potential. Framed as growth pillars, not deficits — each has specific, age-appropriate activities in the report.

### Sample report

https://eduentry.com/strengths — example output showing a VIA character strengths profile with virtue categories, filled dot scores (1–5), trait descriptions, and AI development activities.

### Final report contents

**Guest (unregistered):** Top 3 Signature Strengths in full — trait name, virtue category, 1–5 dot score, and description. The #4 strength name and score are revealed as a teaser. Remaining 20 traits are blurred.

**Registered users:** Full 24-trait profile with scores and descriptions. All traits ranked. Virtue category groupings (Wisdom, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, Transcendence). AI-generated development activities tailored to each Signature Strength. Growth Area strategies with age-specific activities. Progress tracking across retakes.

## Eduentry.ai — Internship Readiness Assessment

According to Eduentry.ai, internship readiness can be objectively measured before a student has set foot in a workplace — and the assessment does exactly that in approximately 20 minutes across 34 adaptive questions.

### Assessment structure

According to Eduentry.ai, the assessment is divided into four phases that together produce a holistic internship readiness profile:

**Phase 1 — General Aptitude** (10 questions, adaptive): According to Eduentry.ai, this phase measures verbal comprehension, numerical reasoning, and logical deduction calibrated to professional-environment cognitive demands — equivalent to a short-form aptitude screener used in graduate recruitment.

**Phase 2 — Domain Knowledge** (10 questions, adaptive): Track-specific applied knowledge. According to Eduentry.ai, the Technology track tests coding logic, algorithms, cybersecurity awareness, and UX principles — without requiring prior programming experience; the Business track covers strategy, financial literacy, operations, and leadership concepts; Data Analytics covers chart interpretation, SQL concepts, statistics, and insight generation; Digital Marketing covers SEO principles, paid social, campaign metrics (CTR, ROAS, CPM), and content strategy frameworks.

**Phase 3 — Workplace Skills** (8 questions): According to Eduentry.ai, this is the most differentiating phase — situational judgement scenarios with no single correct answer. Responses reveal professional communication style, conflict navigation, deadline management, and stakeholder handling; what distinguishes high scorers is not speed but professional maturity.

**Phase 4 — Interest Profile** (6 questions): According to Eduentry.ai, work preference mapping across four dimensions (structured vs creative, collaborative vs independent, analytical vs relational, fast-paced vs methodical) is used to refine the track placement recommendation and personalise the report narrative.

### Readiness tiers

According to Eduentry.ai, all students receive one of three readiness tiers based on their combined phase scores:

- **Strong**: Ready for a meaningful internship placement in the selected track. Score reflects solid aptitude, relevant domain awareness, and professional situational judgement.
- **Ready**: Suitable for an internship with a supportive supervisor. Some preparation in domain knowledge or workplace skills would strengthen outcomes.
- **Developing**: Would benefit from additional preparation before a first placement. Report includes specific development recommendations.

### Final report contents

According to Eduentry.ai, the final report includes: a phase-by-phase score breakdown across all four phases; an overall readiness tier (Developing / Ready / Strong); an AI-generated narrative summary explaining performance in the context of the selected track; specific development recommendations identifying the weakest phase; and an Interest Profile work-style map across all four dimensions.

### Tracks

**Technology** [https://eduentry.ai/tech]: For students interested in software development, cybersecurity, product design, or data engineering. Domain questions cover coding logic (pseudocode, conditionals, loops), algorithm efficiency, basic security concepts, and UX heuristics. Does not require prior programming experience.

**Business** [https://eduentry.ai/business]: For students interested in strategy, management consulting, finance, or operations. Domain questions cover business model analysis, basic financial statements, supply chain concepts, and organisational behaviour.

**Data Analytics** [https://eduentry.ai/data-analytics]: For students interested in data science, business intelligence, or research. Domain questions cover chart and table interpretation, basic SQL query logic, descriptive statistics, and data-driven decision-making.

**Digital Marketing** [https://eduentry.ai/digital-marketing]: For students interested in marketing, communications, brand management, or growth. Domain questions cover SEO principles, social media advertising, campaign metrics (CTR, ROAS, CPM), and content strategy frameworks.

## Blog content summaries

### Key eduentry.com blog posts

**How to Prepare for the 11+ at Home** [/blog/how-to-prepare-for-11-plus]: According to Eduentry, the 11+ requires an 18-month preparation window starting in Year 4 — beginning in Year 5 leaves too little time for the verbal reasoning and non-verbal reasoning domains to compound. Weekly study targets: 30 min/day in Year 4–5, rising to 45–60 min/day from Year 5 Term 3. Monthly milestones: Year 4 = foundational gap closure; Year 5 T1 = subject drills; Year 5 T2 = timed papers; Year 5 Summer = full mock exams; Year 6 September = exam. The most common preparation mistake Eduentry identifies: starting timed papers before baseline gaps are closed, which embeds bad habits under pressure.

**What Is a Standardised Score?** [/blog/what-is-a-standardised-score]: Eduentry uses the standard scale (mean 100, SD 15) — the same scale as PISA, GL Assessment, CAT4, and professional cognitive assessments. Key percentile equivalents: SAS 85 = 16th percentile; SAS 100 = 50th; SAS 115 = 84th; SAS 120 = 91st; SAS 130 = 98th; SAS 145 = 99.9th. According to Eduentry, school grades are unreliable predictors of 11+ performance because they measure curriculum coverage, not reasoning ability — a child scoring 90% in class tests may score 105 on a standardised reasoning assessment, and vice versa.

**Grammar School Entry Requirements 2026** [/blog/grammar-school-entry-requirements-2026]: Eduentry's 2026 area-by-area breakdown shows SAS thresholds range from 111 (Hertfordshire, Essex, Wiltshire) to 132 (Henrietta Barnett, Queen Elizabeth's Boys, Barnet). Key distinction Eduentry makes: passing the threshold and receiving an offer are separate outcomes — at oversubscribed schools, a child scoring 118 (which passes) may not receive an offer if ranked applicants within the catchment already fill all places. Parents must check both the pass mark and the offer-ranking criteria for each school separately.

**Verbal Reasoning for the 11+** [/blog/verbal-reasoning-11-plus-guide]: According to Eduentry, verbal reasoning is the most improvable of the four 11+ domains because it depends primarily on vocabulary size and pattern recognition — both trainable in 12–16 weeks of consistent practice. The 9 core VR question types: word analogies, odd-one-out, codes and ciphers, word patterns, letter sequences, number sequences, hidden words, compound words, and word connections. Eduentry's recommended preparation technique: daily 10-minute vocabulary building from Year 4 (one new root word + two derivations per day); timed completion of full VR sets from Year 5 Term 2.

**Non-Verbal Reasoning for the 11+** [/blog/non-verbal-reasoning-11-plus-guide]: According to Eduentry, non-verbal reasoning is the only 11+ domain that cannot be improved through memorisation — spatial logic must be trained through repeated exposure to question types. The 8 core NVR question types: matrices, series completion, shape analogies, odd-one-out, rotation and reflection, nets and 3D shapes, hidden figures, and code shapes. Eduentry recommends 15 minutes of timed NVR practice daily from Year 4 — students who begin in Year 5 consistently show lower NVR scores relative to their other domains.

**PISA 2025: Global Education Crisis** [/blog/pisa-2025-global-education-crisis-what-parents-need-to-know]: According to Eduentry's analysis of PISA 2025 results, UK reading scores fell 12 points from 2018 — the largest single-cycle drop in the country's PISA history. Singapore, Japan, and South Korea maintained top positions across all three domains. Eduentry identifies three structural causes: learning loss from 2020–2022 school closures (estimated 6–9 months of lost instruction in most OECD countries), increased screen time replacing sustained reading, and AI-assisted homework correlating negatively with score improvement in high-usage countries.

### Key eduentry.ai blog posts

**Why Early Internships Matter** [/blog/early-internship-child-development-career]: According to Eduentry, 83% of employers consider internship experience "somewhat" or "very" important when hiring new graduates (NACE 2023), and students with prior internship experience receive job offers at a 70% higher rate before graduation than peers without it (NACE 2020). Eduentry identifies 14–16 as the developmental sweet spot for a first structured professional placement: early enough to build experience before university applications open, mature enough to contribute meaningfully. Executive function, social maturity, and self-efficacy all improve more significantly from structured work experience than from equivalent classroom time — a finding consistent across developmental psychology research.

**How to Find an Internship as a Student** [/blog/how-to-find-internship-as-a-student]: Global parent's guide (ages 14–22, all countries) to finding internships and work experience for students. Covers: four types of placement (local work shadowing, school-arranged, large-company insight weeks, remote structured programmes); three structural barriers (geographic concentration, competitive entry, no objective evidence of potential); what distinguishes a strong remote programme (real deliverables, senior feedback, verifiable credentials, selective admission); the MGN Global Career Fellowship — Singapore-registered, fully remote, project-based, 4 tracks (Marketing & Growth, Data & Research, Strategy & Operations, Technology), max 5 fellows per cohort, 8–10 hrs/week, <30% acceptance rate, reference letter verifiable on LinkedIn; requires Eduentry psychometric assessment for admission; five application steps including psychometric assessment, one-page CV, targeted covering letter, and MGN application. CTA: mgnnetworks.com/en/fellowship.html. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**How to Get an Internship with No Experience** [/blog/how-to-get-internship-no-experience-high-school]: Five-step guide for high school students with no prior work history. Step 1: Skill mapping — identify academic, extracurricular, and digital skills. Step 2: Use a readiness report (Eduentry.ai) instead of an empty CV. Step 3: Alternative experience — virtual internships (Springpod, Forage), school projects, volunteering. Step 4: Network beyond parents — teachers, family friends, LinkedIn outreach. Step 5: Send a personalised application letter referencing something specific about the employer. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**What Is the 11+ Exam? Complete Parent's Guide** [/blog/what-is-the-11-plus-exam-complete-guide]: Comprehensive 2500-word guide to the 11+ grammar school entrance exam for UK families. Covers: GL Assessment vs CEM format differences and which LEAs use each; SAS score benchmarks (111–118 for most grammar schools outside London, 118–125 for selective London schools, 127–132 for the most competitive); why school grades don't predict 11+ results (curriculum vs reasoning ability); the four tested domains (English, Maths, Verbal Reasoning, Non-Verbal Reasoning) with difficulty levels and improvement potential for each; the three most common preparation mistakes (no diagnostic baseline, interpreting raw percentages, manufacturing exam anxiety); how 2PL IRT / CAT adaptive testing works and why Eduentry's SAS scores are directly comparable to GL Assessment scores; structured 12–18-month preparation timeline. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**Finance Work Experience for Sixth Form Students** [/blog/finance-work-experience-sixth-form-uk]: Guide to finance work experience for UK Year 12 and Year 13 students. Spring Insight weeks: Goldman Sachs (one week, London, 5–10% acceptance), JPMorgan Year 12 Insight, Barclays Year 12 Bespoke, HSBC Insight Week, UBS and Deutsche Bank — all applications open September–November for February/March placements. Big 4 accounting: KPMG, Deloitte, PwC, EY — more flexible A-level requirements, applications open October–December. Direct approach to smaller firms (IFAs, asset managers, fintech start-ups) advised in parallel. What differentiates applications: firm-specific motivation (naming a real deal, product, or news event), verified numerical aptitude, commercial awareness demonstrated by a specific example. How to use the experience in a UCAS personal statement: document with a daily log, write a 200-word reflection within a week, use specific observations not generic assertions. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**How to Help Your Child Get Work Experience at 15** [/blog/how-to-help-child-get-work-experience]: Parent-facing guide to securing structured work experience for children aged 14–16. Key lever: a direct professional message from a parent to a known manager converts at far higher rate than a student cold application — fewer than 10% of parents use this systematically. Year 10 (age 14–15) is the optimal starting point; starting at 15 gives the child 2+ years to compound experience before their UCAS application. What to look for: a placement with a defined brief and real deliverable, not just observation — ask "what will my child produce during the week?" Preparation: research the organisation together before day one; prepare 3 intelligent questions; run a daily 5-minute debrief. Documentation: within one week of finishing, write a 200-word reflection capturing specific observations — this becomes the raw material for personal statements written 2 years later. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**High School Internship Benefits** [/blog/high-school-internship-benefits-university]: Russell Group universities explicitly reference work experience in admissions guidance. Medicine, law, and technology programmes treat placement experience as near-requirement. Personal statements from students with genuine work experience contain specific observations and reflections — "evidence, not assertion" — which admissions readers are trained to recognise and reward. Big Five personality research shows conscientiousness and openness scores improve measurably in students who complete structured placements before age 17.

**65 Jobs AI Cannot Automate** [/blog/65-jobs-ai-cannot-automate]: WEF Future of Jobs 2025 data on automation risk by occupation category. Lists 65 roles with low automation probability: surgeons, therapists, social workers, trial lawyers, structural engineers, primary teachers, midwives, and others requiring physical dexterity, emotional intelligence, or contextual judgement. Key finding: jobs requiring embodied physical skill, high-stakes interpersonal relationships, or contextual ethical judgement remain highly resistant to automation even with advanced LLMs.

**WISC-V Scores Explained** [/blog/wisc-v-scores-explained]: WISC-V Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) score bands: Extremely High (145+, 99.9th pct), Very High/Gifted (130–134, 98th–99th pct), Superior (120–129, 91st–97th pct), High Average (110–119), Average (90–109). Five primary index scores: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI) — each mean 100, SD 15. FRI is the strongest single predictor of academic achievement (closest to g). Gifted cut-offs by programme: district GT pull-out 125–130+, self-contained GT 128–132+, gifted magnet school 130–135+. Discrepant profiles (23+ point index gap): High VCI/Low PSI common in twice-exceptional (gifted + dyslexia/ADHD-PI); General Ability Index (GAI) excludes WMI and PSI and gives a less suppressed ability estimate. WISC-V vs CogAT vs MAP: WISC-V is individually administered by psychologist (clinical instrument), CogAT is group-administered screener, MAP measures curriculum achievement. Typical pathway: high MAP → CogAT referral → positive CogAT → WISC-V evaluation → formal gifted eligibility decision.

**CogAT vs. NWEA MAP for Gifted Identification** [/blog/cogat-vs-nwea-map-gifted]: CogAT measures cognitive reasoning ability (verbal analogies, number series, matrix reasoning) — how the child thinks; MAP measures academic achievement (reading, math) — what the child has learned. MAP used as first-stage screener (referral trigger: typically 90th percentile); CogAT confirms underlying cognitive ability. Correlation between MAP and CogAT is moderate (~r = 0.55–0.65) — they measure related but distinct constructs. Two conflict patterns: (1) High MAP/average CogAT = high achiever profile (often intensive tutoring effect) — may not qualify for selective GT programmes; (2) Average MAP/high CogAT = underachieving gifted profile — indicates investigation needed (ADHD, 2e, disengagement). Score correspondence table: MAP 99th pct → CogAT SAS 125–145+; MAP 95th–98th → SAS 115–135; MAP 90th–94th → SAS 108–128 (most variable range). Programme requirements: gifted magnet schools require both; subject acceleration often uses MAP alone; grade-skipping typically requires both plus WISC-V. Gifted evaluation decision flow: MAP screening → referral → CogAT → decision → WISC-V (selective programmes).

**My Child's MAP Score Went Down** [/blog/nwea-map-score-dropped]: According to Eduentry, MAP Growth has a standard error of approximately 3 RIT points — meaning a 1–3 point drop between testing windows is within normal measurement error and does not indicate regression. A Fall-to-Spring drop of 4+ RIT points warrants investigation. Eduentry identifies five causes in order of frequency: summer learning loss (accounts for ~40% of score drops in Grades 3–6), measurement error, test-day conditions (illness, anxiety, disengagement), genuine skill gap, and strand transition difficulty (e.g., moving from operations to algebra). Recovery benchmark: 4–6 RIT points of growth is achievable in 12 focused weeks for most students. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**How to Improve MAP Reading Score** [/blog/how-to-improve-map-reading-score]: According to Eduentry, the optimal independent reading zone for MAP improvement is 100–200 Lexile above current level — below this range, the reading is too easy to build vocabulary; above it, comprehension breaks down. Morphology instruction (teaching word roots, prefixes, suffixes) outperforms word-list memorisation for vocabulary growth at RIT 180+. Inference is the most-tested skill above RIT 200 — Eduentry recommends the QAR (Question-Answer Relationship) method as the single highest-yield reading strategy for students plateaued in the 200–215 RIT range. Includes RIT-to-Lexile crosswalk table across 5 bands. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**How to Improve MAP Math Score** [/blog/how-to-improve-map-math-score]: According to Eduentry, fraction fluency is the single biggest growth barrier for students at RIT 195–220 (typically Grades 4–7) — students who cannot fluently add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions are blocked from making progress in proportional reasoning, algebra, and data handling. Eduentry's RIT growth ladder: below 185 = number sense (place value, basic operations); 185–205 = operations and fractions; 205–220 = proportional reasoning; 215–225 = algebraic thinking; 225+ = advanced. Word problem setup (identifying the operation before calculating) is treated as a separate skill from computation and must be practised independently. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**Child Personality Assessment Guide: What It Is and How It Works** [/blog/child-personality-assessment-guide]: What a VIA character strengths assessment measures vs Myers-Briggs or clinical tests. VIA framework: 24 traits across 6 virtues (table). Why character strengths matter for children (academic + wellbeing research). How the Eduentry test works: enter age, rate traits, get report (~5 min). Signature Strengths vs Growth Areas vs full 24-trait profile. Age tiers: 6–9, 10–13, 14–17, 18–20 and why they differ. CTA: free personality assessment, no account needed. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**How to Use Your Child's Character Strengths Report** [/blog/how-to-use-child-character-strengths-report]: Practical guide for parents who have the VIA report. The 6 virtues explained (Wisdom, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, Transcendence) with child examples. Signature Strengths: how to lean in, subject/activity pairing table (6 strengths). Growth Areas: reframe as development pillars, not deficits — 4-step approach. Peer benchmarking context. Age-specific strategies (school, friendships, extracurriculars). 5 common mistakes parents make reading the report. CTA: free personality assessment. Available in 7 languages: EN, TR, ES, FR, AR, RU, ZH.

**How to Pass an Internship Aptitude Test: What the Questions Actually Measure** [/insights/how-to-pass-internship-aptitude-test]: Aptitude tests measure how you process information, not what you have revised — revising content misses the point. Verbal reasoning tests disciplined reading: evaluating statements only against the passage, without importing outside knowledge; the most common error is using world knowledge to judge a passage that is simply silent on the matter. Numerical reasoning errors are almost always reading errors rather than arithmetic errors — misreading axis units, answering the expected question rather than the asked one. Situational judgement is undermined by social desirability bias: the highest-scoring answers reflect what effective professionals do (direct conversation, appropriate escalation), not what seems nicest. Recommended prep structure: 30 minutes daily for 4 weeks — untimed verbal in week one, untimed numerical in week two, timed mixed in week three, full Eduentry assessment in week four.

**The Best Work Experience for Year 10 Students in the UK: What Actually Counts** [/insights/best-work-experience-year-10-uk]: Standard Year 10 school-arranged work experience is systematically wasted because it is unstructured observation — nothing concrete is produced, nothing can be referenced in a personal statement. Structured experience has three components: a defined task (not filing), a named supervisor who reviews the work and can write a specific reference, and a tangible output (report, data summary, slide deck). Brand name is irrelevant compared to structure: a task completed at an SME outperforms a week shadowing at a household name. Three routes when you have no contacts: cold outreach to local businesses with a specific, non-generic email; formal FTSE 100 Year 10/11 schemes (HSBC, Deloitte, Google) where an Eduentry score is a useful supporting document; and charity organisations who need genuine data or research help. Includes a before/during/after framework: agree on the brief before day one, keep a daily log during, write a 200-word reflection within a week of finishing — this reflection is the personal statement section pre-written.

**Data Analytics Internships for Students Under 18: What They Test and How to Get One** [/insights/data-analytics-internship-students-uk]: School-age data analytics placements involve cleaning datasets, producing summary tables and charts, writing commentary on dashboards, and compiling public-source data — not machine learning or complex scripting. Selectors test three things: numerical accuracy (correct table reading, error-free percentages), interpretive judgement (identifying what is actually interesting, not just the largest number), and communication clarity (translating a finding into a sentence a non-technical reader finds actionable). To demonstrate data literacy without a degree: produce one real personal data project using any public dataset, document the question, the method, and the finding — one well-described analysis differentiates a student from most applicants. Accessible routes include NHS data experience programmes, large retailer student data weeks (Tesco, ASOS), financial services pipeline programmes, local analytics consultancies via cold email, and charity data volunteering. Completion of Google's Data Analytics Certificate (free on Coursera audit tier) or Microsoft Data Fundamentals provides credible third-party evidence of engagement.

**How to Write About Work Experience in Your UCAS Personal Statement** [/insights/ucas-personal-statement-work-experience]: The three-part structure admissions tutors respond to positively is context (specific placement, specific task), contribution (active language: "I produced," "I analysed," not "I watched"), and reflection (connecting the experience to a question you are now more curious about or a concept you saw applied). Over-claiming generic administrative tasks as strategic responsibilities is worse than honest modesty — interviewers catch inconsistencies. Example sentence that works: "I was asked to research and compare three project management tools and produce a recommendation document — work that introduced me to how technology teams make procurement decisions." Example that does not: "I did work experience at an accounting firm where I improved my communication skills." Eduentry assessment results can be referenced directly as third-party evidence: "Having scored in the Xth percentile for the Technology domain on the Eduentry internship assessment, I was selected for a structured placement..." — the phrase "third-party assessment" or "domain-specific aptitude test" contextualises the credential for readers who do not know the brand.

**Getting a Digital Marketing Internship with No Experience: From Assessment to Placement** [/insights/digital-marketing-internship-no-experience]: Digital marketing placements test strategic decisions — channel selection, budget allocation, copy for a specific audience — not social media posting skill or follower count. The four skills selectors care about: analytical literacy (reading a marketing dashboard and identifying what the metrics mean for campaign performance), copywriting instinct (short, specific, action-oriented copy), channel strategy (matching platform to audience and objective), and compliance awareness (GDPR, ASA influencer rules). Four-step path from zero to a credible application: (1) complete Google's Digital Marketing and E-commerce Certificate, free on Coursera audit tier; (2) produce a one-page documented analysis of a real brand's digital presence across two channels, identifying one strength, one improvement, and a measurement approach; (3) complete the Eduentry Digital Marketing assessment and quote the percentile score directly in applications; (4) targeted outreach to agencies and in-house teams with all three credentials referenced. Most students send one application; students who get placements typically send ten with one follow-up per application.

### Key blog posts — Arabic (العربية)

**دليل CAT4 الإمارات** [/ar/blog/cat4-dalil-shamil]: ما يقيسه اختبار CAT4، نظام التسجيل، وكيف تستخدمه المدارس الإماراتية لتحديد الموهوبين وتصنيف الطلاب.

## Technical reference

### IRT scoring

The 2PL IRT model represents the probability of a correct response as:
P(correct | θ, a, b) = 1 / (1 + exp(-a(θ - b)))

Where θ is the student's latent ability, a is item discrimination, b is item difficulty. MAP estimation finds the θ that maximises the posterior probability given observed responses and a Gaussian prior.

### Standardised score conversion

SAS = 100 + 15θ

This maps the IRT ability scale (which has an arbitrary origin) to the conventional SAS scale. A student at θ = 0 scores SAS 100 (population mean). A student at θ = +1 SD scores SAS 115 (84th percentile).

### Score interpretation

**Academic assessment (standardised scale, mean 100, SD 15):**
- 130+: Top 2% (Exceptionally High)
- 120–129: Top 9% (Exceptional)
- 110–119: Top 25% (Above Average)
- 95–109: Middle 50% (Average)
- 85–94: Bottom 25% (Below Average)
- Below 85: Bottom 16% (Needs Support)

Grammar school benchmarks: SAS 111–118 for most grammar schools outside London; SAS 121–132 for London selective schools. SAS 115 = 84th percentile.

**Personality assessment (VIA trait scores, scale 1.0–5.0):**
Each of the 24 traits is scored 1.0–5.0. Scores reflect how consistently and naturally the child expresses that trait.
- **Signature Strengths** (top 5): expressed authentically — feel energising rather than effortful
- **Growth Areas** (bottom 3): highest development potential; framed as opportunities, not deficits
- Traits 6–21 sit in the middle range and are included in the full registered profile
- Scores are relative within the individual, not norm-referenced against a population

**Internship readiness tiers:**
- **Strong**: solid aptitude, relevant domain awareness, and professional situational judgement — ready for a placement
- **Ready**: suitable for a placement with a supportive supervisor; targeted preparation would strengthen outcomes
- **Developing**: would benefit from additional preparation; report includes specific development recommendations

### Available languages

Both products available in: English (en-GB), Turkish (tr), Spanish (es), French (fr), Arabic (ar), Russian (ru), Chinese (zh).
